quote: Welches ist die Discriminante jener Gl.?
english: What is the discriminant of that equation?
topic: Three short notes: questions on the discriminant of a quadratic form built from the roots of an algebraic equation (the equation with real roots in lambda), a question on directly proving regularity of solutions of differential equations other than Laplace's, and the problem of counting the possible configurations of n circles in the plane.

triage.modern_statement: This is my best reading of the note, not a certain one. Hilbert builds a real quadratic form, i.e. a real symmetric matrix A, from the roots of an algebraic equation. He then looks at the equation det(A − λI) = 0, which is known to have only real roots in λ, and asks what its discriminant is. In modern terms: give an explicit formula for the discriminant of the characteristic polynomial of a real symmetric matrix, as a polynomial in the matrix entries. That discriminant is ∏_{i<j}(λ_i − λ_j)^2. Hilbert may also have meant the more specific question of how its structure explains why all the roots are real.
triage.answered_by: If the reading is right, the question was already answered before Hilbert wrote it. Kummer (1843) wrote the discriminant for 3×3 symmetric matrices explicitly as a sum of squares. Borchardt (1846) showed it is a sum of squares for every n, which shows directly that the roots are real. Later refinements: Ilyushechkin (1992, Mat. Zametki) treated normal matrices; Parlett (2002) wrote the discriminant as a determinant; Domokos (2011, Comm. Pure Appl. Math.) found sharper sum-of-squares representations, with a minimum of 5 squares for 3×3 and 7 squares for 4×4. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: The discriminant of n×n real symmetric matrices is a sum of squares, with as many terms as the dimension of the space of n-variable spherical harmonics of degree n. For 3×3 it needs exactly five squares; for 4×4, seven squares suffice. These results improve on Kummer (1843) and Borchardt (1846).

Kummer gave an explicit sum-of-squares formula for n=3 and Borchardt showed the discriminant is a sum of squares for every n. The discriminant can also be written as a determinant (Parlett), with an elementary proof of Ilyushechkin's result.

triage.why: The note is very short, and 'jener Gl.' (that equation) refers to an equation elsewhere on the page that I could not see. My guess is that it is the λ-equation (characteristic, or secular, equation) of the quadratic form built from the roots, as in the Hermite/Jacobi construction. That fits the page description of an equation with real roots in λ. Under that reading, the discriminant was already known in Hilbert's time to be a sum of squares (Kummer 1843, Borchardt 1846). The minimum number of squares needed was later worked out by Ilyushechkin and Domokos. Some follow-up work continues: the search results include more recent papers that build on this sum-of-squares structure. However, the sources I found don't show whether this counts as an active area, so I marked it 'unclear'. If 'that equation' means a different equation, I cannot identify the question.
